items.question: Why do you think building useful AI agents requires rethinking pre-training from fundamentals?
items.object: Rethinking pre-training for agentic AI
items.answer: For the longest time, we were measuring pre-training on static benchmarks. If we want these models to be useful as agents, they need to be able to interact with environments. And when we start caring about those agentic tasks, pre-training needs to rethink from fundamentals. This is not just a post-training problem to achieve these set of capabilities that we want in the next generation of models. And the kind of benchmarks we need for measuring this kind of intelligence is sometimes not available today.

items.question: Why do you find thinking across the stack essential to pre-training a model?
items.object: Thinking across the stack in model pre-training
items.answer: One thing that I find super interesting about pre-training is that you have to be able to think across the stack. If you're going to train something for two or two and a half months, you need to be able to think about every single part of the system.

items.question: Why do you think building useful AI agents requires rethinking pre-training?
items.object: Rethinking pre-training for agentic AI
items.answer: Well, the way I really put it is that for the longest time we were measuring pre-training on static benchmarks. For example, LU is a popular one, or GSM8K or Math Olympiad problems like AIME and math, or you name it, but extremely static benchmarks. If you want these models to be useful as agents, they need to be able to interact with environments and be useful to us in the workflows where we can use them. The simplest versions of that that we are already starting to see today are coding agents and deep research agents. The coding agents are extremely useful in the sense that you can put a coding agent to help you understand a large code base, or they can help you, for example, to refactor and apply a fix across multiple files. They might not do it correctly. They're not perfect yet. In deep research agents, I think we moved away from just a search bar interface to more like, here is what you want, and then putting a language model on the job of finding multiple articles that investigate that kind of workflow. You can imagine that any such goal-oriented task can be given to the language models, and the models can achieve these goals over multiple steps as opposed to just being chatbots. So those are the kind of agentic tasks that we start caring about. And when we start caring about those agentic tasks, pre-training needs to rethink from fundamentals. This is not just a post-training problem to achieve these set of capabilities that we want in the next generation of models. And the kind of benchmarks we need for measuring this kind of intelligence is sometimes not available today.

items.question: Why do you see relying on post-training to develop agentic AI as limiting?
items.object: The limits of relying on post-training to develop agentic AI
items.answer: Oh, we totally can keep doing that. I think it's limiting in the sense that it fundamentally limits you in what you can achieve in terms of capabilities. The way I think about models is: what are they capable of? The capabilities can be anything from, do they have long-context capabilities? Can they do retrieval over longer context? Are they good at, for example, solving natural language understanding problems? Are they good at natural language generation problems? Are they good at reasoning? I think what is especially important about agentic tasks like coding tasks is that if you're trying to read a codebase and then execute some parts of it or write about it, you will accumulate context over time because you're reading a lot of content, and then if you execute something, you also have some additional feedback from execution. So what you need a model to be able to do is have planning as a capability, have the ability to reason over its context length, which might be very long. What went well, what did not go well. It needs to be able to fail from trajectories that went wrong, for example. So it can have short-term setbacks where it went and did something wrong, but then it needs to correct course for itself. And then it needs to be able to learn new tools on the go. It needs to be able to explore tools and figure out what it should use if it's put in new environments. So all of this is possible to some extent, but it's sometimes limited. The fundamental problem where you see it's very limiting is the context engineering problem. When companies build agentic systems today, they are building it by doing a lot of context engineering. They tack on a lot of things; it's literally limited to this is what I can fit into context length, and that's the length my agent will do, and then the next thing will be the next sub-agent.

items.question: How do you think pre-training needs to be reconsidered to give language models stronger long-form reasoning capabilities?
items.object: Rethinking pre-training for long-form reasoning
items.answer: When I go and talk about rethinking pre-training, I always think about it in terms of what are the capabilities we want out of the models. To me, architecture is just one part of the equation. A big part of the equation is what is the loss objective and what is the training data. As I was alluding to before, what we want are these models to be able to do planning and reasoning over multiple steps, look at what they did in their context before and refer to that, and use that as a way to inform their next steps in terms of taking actions. For them to be able to do that, the fundamental mechanism in transformers that enables this is the attention mechanism. Whether the attention mechanism works well over long context or not is a question that we're definitely taking a very strong look at, as to whether that's the best way for us to achieve long-form reasoning. We do know that long-form retrieval, like if you want to retrieve over millions of context length, is achievable today with large language models. Reasoning over longer context is a harder problem. The second bit that's extremely important is the training data that goes into these models. And the third bit that's extremely important is the loss objectives. Believe it or not, we have actually trained these models to probabilistically predict the next token. What is the most likely next token? Out of that we have managed to get these models to be extremely strong reasoners. But is that the best objective one could go after, embedding the fact that we need these models to have more fundamental long-form reasoning capabilities and need to be able to learn how to learn from their contexts?

items.question: Why do you think model pre-training tends to see incremental changes while post-training sees more radical changes?
items.object: Risk and incremental change in model pre-training
items.answer: I think you have to have gone through the pre-training experience for multiple generations of models to know where to make the bets. Pre-training is one of the sciences which is both fun and exciting and high risk at high capital expenditure. So when you make those bets, you want to be as sure of your bet as possible, and that's why pre-training sees most incremental changes and post-training sees more radical changes, as my experience. Otherwise you spend a lot more time debugging through what you changed as opposed to getting a model that works.

items.question: How do you assess promising model architectures whose researchers leave scaling to someone else?
items.object: Scaling proposed model architectures
items.answer: There are a lot of interesting proposed architectures that I come across where the researcher is leaving scaling to someone else because they don't have the resources, but it still leaves a big question as to whether you'll see the expected results at scale. I think for folks who are experienced in scaling and have had the fortune of being one, it's truly an art and a science to get it right. It's not just like we change this thing and we change this other thing and it just works. It's a fun adventure every single time.

items.question: How do you think attention mechanisms need to evolve to support agentic capabilities?
items.object: Attention mechanisms for agentic AI
items.answer: When I think about agentic capabilities, I think the fundamental bit that we need out of the attention mechanism—and I'm not proposing exactly the solution—is the ability to look at not just things around its context length but also being able to refer to things that were further in the past. For specific examples of, say, deep research agents, you might have collected 100 articles, and then you need to somehow organize them into topics. Your attention mechanism needs to have some form of a summary of these articles, in that it needs to somehow organize them into content that is a synthesized report that you will give to the user. A lot of the heavy lifting in this case is being done by the attention mechanism. How do you think about that long-form reasoning? What is the token attending to? Is that enough or not enough? Those are the kind of questions we ask.

items.question: How do you see the role of memory tools relative to attention mechanisms in large language models?
items.object: Memory tools and attention mechanisms in large language models
items.answer: I think I see memory as an additional tool in addition to the attention mechanism. At any given point in time, what we want the language models to be able to reason well about is what tool to use, memory being one of them. As long as they are strong reasoners, they should be able to refer back to an index and say, this is where I need to look up content, and this is what I need to go back and read from the context length. Today, the way some of these systems end up being engineered are as multi-agent systems where you put sub-agents and something is going to go fetch that content. Effectively, what you're referring to is the ability of the large language model to use a tool which can look up a database or memory or something that's perhaps stored away. That's how humans do it, right? That type of memory approach doesn't necessarily remove the requirement to have a different approach to attention that enables different recall models, I guess.

items.question: How do you think about choosing a model architecture for training at scale?
items.object: Model architecture choices at scale
items.answer: For me, there has to be a good reason, and one has to be extremely rigorous about evaluations. One has to be extremely rigorous about the way you do scaling. Innocuous changes that feel fun and exciting don't work at scale. So there has to be a good reason to make that bet. Every single bet is extremely well vetted. Consequently, Transformers have been extremely well vetted relative to the next best thing.

items.question: How do you think about pre-training objectives for language models that need to act as agents?
items.object: Pre-training objectives for agentic language models
items.answer: There are ways that we might want to tweak attention, but it's only one part of the pre-training recipe. There's also fine-tuning the loss. If I think about next-token prediction for an LLM and think about the initial tasks that we expected LLMs to do, like generate text, that makes sense. It's intuitive. When we think about agents, there are so many more things that we need these agents to be good at. Reasoning is one thing that you mentioned. Tool use is another.

items.question: How do you think the move toward agentic AI changes the division between pre-training and post-training?
items.object: The division between pre-training and post-training for agentic AI
items.answer: I would say it unifies the two paradigms. I think pre- and post-training fundamentally comes from the world of: we had to start out with pre-training because that's where we saw scaling gave us the largest set of gains in amplifying the natural language capabilities, while post-training allowed us to make these models more accessible as chatbots. They were extremely strong when you got them working with, say, reinforcement learning with human feedback. As we move into this agentic paradigm, is reasoning a capability you want to endow in the model in the last stage, or does that move up front, and do we need a very strict divide between the two paradigms? That's a great question to ask.

items.question: How do you see the role of training-data curation in making pre-trained models more compute efficient?
items.object: Training-data curation for pre-trained models
items.answer: Pre-trained models are fundamentally dependent on large volumes of data that is high quality and diverse. I think the bit that we have exploited the most is go for as much scale as possible. More and more data is always better, and go for as diverse data sources as possible. I think what we have seen from our counterparts in the east—Qwen models or our DeepSeek models or Kimi models—is that the quality of curation in training data matters as well. That is one axis in which you get a lot more compute efficiency out of pre-trained models when you get your training data to be extremely high quality.

items.question: What do you see as the central challenge in using reasoning traces as pre-training data?
items.object: Reasoning traces as pre-training data
items.answer: The second axis that matters is more along the axis of reasoning. How do you get really good reasoning traces? It's almost like asking the question today: if you train on the internet, reasoning emerges kind of by default, but how do you get those expert traces of people working on problems in all possible domains? Today we are doing them by getting these models to explore in reinforcement learning environments and whatnot. But once we have some semblance of understanding how these models can generate those traces, what should we put in and what is available at scale and pre-training starts to become a question. This alludes to the fact that what would be good reasoning traces that can feed back into the models at large scale is a question that we're thinking a lot about.

items.question: How do you think reasoning-oriented training data can reach volumes comparable to the dominant sources used in pre-training?
items.object: Augmenting existing pre-training data sources to produce reasoning-oriented training data at scale
items.answer: I think the question that is worth asking is: what is the dominant pre-training data source, and how can that be augmented to generate that kind of volume of data? There are some pointers in that direction. For example, the dominant training data source would end up being, say, articles on the internet. How do you use articles on the internet too, but augment them in interesting ways? There have been some results which show that you can formulate them into question-answer pairs or conversational sort of things, or if you have problem-solving tasks, then you can augment them in interesting ways. There is starting to be work in this direction, but you have to tap into the fundamental volumes of data to generate similar volumes of data before we can go down the path of completely new generated data sources.

items.object: The underlying data distribution when training models on synthetic data

items.question: How do you think benchmarks should measure the capabilities of agentic models?
items.object: Benchmarks for agentic model capabilities
items.answer: The fun thing about benchmarks is that every year there are a few new ones that come out and then they get saturated, and then you have to build a new set of benchmarks. For a lot of the frontier development for these models, the current paradigm that we have kind of settled on is that everyone builds benchmarks in-house to measure what is the set of model capabilities they're going after. I was alluding to the fact that, for example, we want these models to be able to reason better in long-form reasoning over their context length. We want them to be able to do multi-step problems. They need to be able to tackle not just the next step but what their actions might be in multiple steps from now. We want these models to be able to recover from failed trajectories, plan better, and learn how to use tools. All of these capabilities require very specific ways of measuring. Even though I'm giving you overarching concepts, when you break them down and put them, for example, in actual coding tasks or in benchmark-style tasks, we're starting to see some of these tasks with varying horizons come into picture. METR has this software atomic actions thing that allows you to have task lengths, and there are a few other benchmarks. You basically want tasks that are varying in complexity and also varying along these dimensions of capability to test the models. It's almost like if you were to break down your real workflow in a day: what are the sub-processes that the models could go after, or what are the sub-sub-problems that the model could go after? Even if those are hard, why is it hard? Making that a challenge for the model is roughly how a lot of these benchmarks are constructed.

items.question: What did testing PaLM on a crowdsourced reasoning benchmark teach you about the value of having many different benchmarks?
items.object: Discovering PaLM's reasoning capabilities through benchmarks
items.answer: To give you a sense of why this is super important: three or four years ago, when we were training PaLM, it was a large model, but we tried this on a new benchmark that was crowdsourced through researchers who were basically coming up with reasoning tasks that they found large language models could not do back in the day. We tried our freshly trained, actually halfway-trained model on this benchmark. What we found was suddenly this benchmark had a step change, and that led us down the path of figuring out the model was actually starting to showcase reasoning capabilities. That's fascinating to some extent, but that would not really have been available had we not had that plethora of benchmarks to look at, including understanding emojis or how does the model reason over a movie script or whatnot. These questions, sourcing these questions in the right ways and understanding what is hard with the current generation of models, is often the way to make progress towards the next set.

items.question: How do you approach planning pre-training when benchmarks for real-world LLM workflows are still evolving?
items.object: Planning pre-training around fundamental model capabilities and evolving benchmarks
items.answer: The fundamental set of capabilities that I talked about, which is roughly three or four that I can count on one hand, are things that if we believe those are fundamental paths, we'll definitely prioritize them. In addition to the usual array of benchmarks, I also believe that we are just at the start of getting reinforcement learning to work well with LLMs. The first reasoning model with reinforcement learning really came out a year ago. I do believe that a lot of the workflows that are being tried out in the real world will make it into benchmarks over the next year. So we will have more benchmarks that are representative of real-world workflows that will test the models in challenging ways and help us learn where the models are challenged versus not. The fun part about planning pre-training is that it ends up being a longer-term endeavor. You have to think ahead of time of what the fundamental model capabilities you're shooting for and plan for that.

items.question: How do you think about the role of larger-scale models in your pursuit of capable, cost-efficient models?
items.object: Model scaling and the pursuit of capable, cost-efficient models
items.answer: When you go for larger-scale models, you often find capabilities much sooner than you will in smaller models. Typically, model scaling is one way in which we notice model capabilities that we haven't noticed before. Often the model capabilities that become available at scale then, with the right training data and the right set of things and training longer and whatnot, become available in smaller models as well. O4 Mini came out after the largest reasoning model was constructed out of, say, I don't know the specifics, but let's assume GPT-4, right? You take the largest models, post-train them for reasoning, and then the next generation of models had that capability even in the smaller models. What I would say and what we are shooting for is the most capable models, and then the most cost-efficient, most capable models. Often, to discover that capability, you do have to go to the right scale, and then you can come back and make them cost-efficient. Often that involves an additional step of distilling, which helps. That's the way to look at it.

items.question: How do you understand the role of larger language models in discovering capabilities that can later appear in smaller models?
items.object: Emergence of capabilities in large language models
items.answer: Often, at least in my track record and history of playing with large language models and training them, emergence is something that you find: fun and interesting things in the larger models, and then you often distill them or get them in the smaller models in the next generation because you figured out exactly the recipe that it takes to get them.

items.question: How do you distinguish long-form reasoning across a model's context from retrieving relevant information?
items.object: Long-form reasoning across a model's context
items.answer: I'll give you very specific examples of what is long-form. If you wanted an AI model, for the longest time you might want an AI to understand your entire codebase, including the parts of the codebase that another team wrote. Perhaps if you have a large enough organization, you basically wanted it to go look at different parts of the codebase, and anytime you tap on that particular subset of the codebase you want to be able to understand it. What long-form would allow you to do is, for this part of the codebase that your team is working on, you can reference that part of the codebase and use it like a library without thinking about it, because AI can help you understand it and use it seamlessly. You don't actually have to walk up to that team and spend time finding team members there. That's one form of long-form reasoning. What that roughly means is if you put a lot of these things in context, the model is able to reason about a disparate set of things that are pretty far apart in position in the context. Another way to look at it—and that is a hard problem—is that for the longest time, if you just want to retrieve relevant parts of the codebase, that's an easier problem for the models to solve. Needle in a haystack, or multiple needles in a haystack, is a problem. But when you go to benchmarks that have multi-hop reasoning, say MRCV2 or LoFT, these benchmarks have only recently started to show signal that models are getting better. For the longest time, these were not the benchmarks where you were seeing strong capabilities even in very long-context models. Even though you have millions of tokens in your context length, you're not necessarily able to think about all of them. If you put in a very confusing set of documents, like let's say you want to do deep research and go on a vacation and you have 10 articles about your favorite vacation spot, the model will not necessarily always be able to think about each one of those articles and give you a synthesized form from each one of them. That's a harder problem for the model to solve. That's one form of long-term reasoning that we're talking about.

items.question: What do you see as the missing capabilities in current models' reasoning over trajectories?
items.object: Long-form reasoning over trajectories
items.answer: The second form of long-term reasoning that I'm talking about is more along the side of trajectories. When you want the models to do multi-step reasoning, what you're asking of the models is to think ahead. It's like the game of chess, where you are thinking ahead and the next action that you take should move you, or at least have some sense of projection of where it will take you towards your goal. That bit has not existed because they're realistically just generating the next token. How do you reason about where this next set of tokens will take you? What does that mean in terms of trajectories with the next action that you take? Those are also bits that have not existed. Or how was the past affecting up to this point in time? If you're looking at an existing trajectory where there are failures and then recover from that, often the models will get stuck in repetitive loops today because they don't really know that they made that failure. They'll go try that same thing again because that's the most probabilistic thing to go through. Those are some examples of long-form reasoning that are pretty pertinent in today's generation of models.

items.question: How do you understand the challenge of getting an AI agent to learn from failed steps while carrying out a task?
items.object: AI agents learning from failed steps in task trajectories
items.answer: Let me define the word trajectories. Let's say you are solving a coding task in Terminal Bench or SWE-bench, or you're solving a goal-oriented task in general. We will have come up with a plan of the relevant set of files to go look at, the set of changes that would help achieve the objective, and then you would go try those changes. Then you would have some form of a verification process where you would go run tests, for example, to verify whether these changes will solve the problem or not. When you collect such traces, where here was the relevant context, here was my solution to the problem, here is what I tried, and here is the output, the execution feedback from trying this, what you'll find is that over multiple steps the model might need to figure out what it learned from the past step should not be redone, or it should choose a different set of actions in the subsequent set of steps. That's a harder problem for the model both from the perspective of paying attention—these are a discrete set of things, so it needs to choose a new action space. That's partly a reinforcement learning problem, but it's also a pre-training problem: what was the model paying attention to? Did it understand that these were failed steps? Were the trajectories passed in the right format so that it noticed that these were things to correct on? It's both a reinforcement learning objective problem, but it's as much a problem of what is the length of context the model is able to pay attention to and learn from.

items.question: How do you think about hallucination in a language model?
items.object: Language model hallucination
items.answer: I see hallucination as more of what probabilistically was the highest-probability next set of tokens that the model thought it should output. To me, was there anything else that could have made it into its context, or could it have gotten additional feedback from interacting with a set of tools to change course in certain ways? That's the question I'm asking: given the goal and the history of all the things that it has tried to achieve that objective, is there a next set of probabilistic tokens that it can output that would have a higher probability of moving it forward towards the goal?

items.question: How do you envision a model responding when it lacks enough information to verify its proposed solution?
items.object: A model verifying a proposed solution when it lacks enough information
items.answer: So yes, it doesn't have enough information to verify what it proposed is the correct solution. So it goes and tries a few other ways to verify the approach that it was trying, and then comes back and it's like, okay, now I have enough information to make an informed decision.

items.question: Why do you see learning new tools through exploration and feedback as a promising direction for AI agents?
items.object: Agents learning new tools through exploration and feedback
items.answer: I think what we have taught our models to kind of learn so far is really what we put in context is what they know. If we could point them in the direction of, here are tools, and by interaction they are able to learn how these tools are useful versus not, that is something that has been tried in the past in the form of continual learning or in the world of robotics, like watch by imitation. Watch by how this tool is being used. The question comes back to how can we get the models to meta-learn, learn how to learn? What exactly is the format in which this exploration of the new environment needs to be done so that the model learns to take actions in that space? One of the promising directions there has been some form of unified domain-specific language, perhaps in code format, that would allow for this kind of reasoning to emerge. There have been a few papers in that direction. Overall, I do believe that the ability to explore new tools and learn by exploration and feedback from trying those tools allows for more flexible and capable models than literally either having to fit them all in context length, having to fine-tune them with all the right traces, or pruning the set of tools that goes into the context so that you have the perfect system built to go in. I think there is a fair bit of work to happen to get that bit going. It's not off-the-shelf available today.

items.question: How do you see the principles behind coding agents applying to agents for enterprise or consumer workflows?
items.object: Applying coding-agent principles to workflow agents
items.answer: I do believe the same principles apply, though slightly broader. Even when we are building coding agents, and even before that when we were building large language models, one of the fundamental capabilities that we get at pre-training scale is that the models learn to reason across modalities. What that means is they learn to reason across languages, across code and text, and across different languages even within code, or even modalities that are not text. To us, the fundamental principles for building anything that requires reasoning across a crossover set of domains comes from this kind of capability. To me, the fundamental principles still very much apply, and it's mostly a matter of maybe the last stage of post-training will be different. The models need to be able to reason across domains, across text and language, across different domains or languages and so on.

items.question: How do you see Reflection’s research team as an environment for someone interested in building open agentic models?

items.answer: Our mission is to build frontier open intelligence. We are a team of about 60 researchers, so very small still, hoping to build a frontier lab for open agentic models. items.question: How do you think researchers can use evaluation benchmarks to make a meaningful contribution to improving language models?
items.object: Evaluation benchmarks as a starting point for improving language models
items.answer: I think a lot of the work starts with building good systems of measurement. A lot of what I talked about are capabilities that don't really have fundamentally strong benchmarks that actually measure them. The best way to think about measuring intelligence is that often you think, if I could use this language model for this particular thing, and then you actually find the model is not good at it. That's a starting point: why is it not good at it? What is missing in the models today? Being able to create that in a packaged form—and these are evaluation benchmarks that don't work well—is often a very good starting point. I spend time at Stanford as well. Often I'll work with students to figure out where are the gaps in the current set of models. How does that lead to an evaluation benchmark that we can use? From there you can start with post-training, which is a relatively inexpensive shift for you to go try and see what gaps you can already start to close in the models. If that excites you, then come join us, or set out on your path to take on a bigger adventure to build these models from scratch.
